title: RBAC v2 (Private) — Policy bundle distribution + update notes (incl. air-gapped)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
Private deployments can’t assume always-on connectivity to Redwood-hosted control plane. RBAC v2 policies (default roles + permissions + action taxonomy) ship as a “policy bundle” that must be:
- installable on day 0 (fresh install)
- updatable on upgrades (and occasionally as a patch)
- verifiable (integrity + provenance)
- compatible across version skew (policy bundle vs control plane binaries vs console UI)
- supportable in air-gapped environments

This is a working doc for possible distribution designs + tradeoffs. Not final.


Terminology (quick)
- Private control plane: customer-hosted Redwood control plane services + console backend deployed into customer environment.
- Policy bundle: versioned artifact containing RBAC v2 schema + default role definitions + action allowlists + optional reason code mappings and metadata.
- Evaluator: runtime library/service that loads bundle and answers allow/deny.
- “Installer”: our private deployment installer/upgrade tool (currently used for templates + config + images; name varies by customer).


Assumptions / constraints
1) Air-gapped customers: no outbound network; upgrades happen via customer importing artifacts (container images, helm charts, tarballs).
2) Private must be auditable: we need a story for “what policy was in effect at time T?” and “who changed it?” (ties to Kevin’s audit log fields: policy_version + decision info).
3) Version skew will happen:
   - customer upgrades console/control-plane later than policy updates, or vice versa
   - customer has multiple environments (dev/stage/prod) on different versions
   - support may request temporary policy patches to unblock customers (we must avoid ad-hoc edits that break signatures).
4) We need a safe rollback story (upgrade fails or policy causes unexpected denies).
5) Enterprise asks: ability to map SSO groups -> roles; and future custom roles (not necessarily in v0, but policy distribution should not paint us into a corner).


Goals (Private-specific)
- G1: Policy bundle is always present locally; evaluator does not require external calls.
- G2: Bundle integrity is verifiable offline (signature verification) and fails closed or “safe degraded” in a controlled way.
- G3: Upgrades are deterministic: installer can stage a new bundle, verify it, apply it atomically, and rollback.
- G4: Version skew handling is explicit: services can detect policy schema compatibility and surface actionable errors.
- G5: Bundle update path works for:
  (a) regular product upgrades
  (b) emergency security patch to policy bundle (rare)

Non-goals (for now)
- Not designing full custom-role authoring UI for Private customers in this doc.
- Not changing SSO/SAML integration architecture; only mapping group claims to roles.
- Not solving data-plane inference authorization beyond tenant/project scoping.


What is inside the bundle? (proposed)
Bundle is an immutable archive with:
- manifest.json (or YAML) with:
  - bundle_version (semver)
  - policy_schema_version (semver)
  - built_at timestamp
  - min_control_plane_version / max_control_plane_version (or compatibility range)
  - hash of each file
  - signing metadata (key id)
- roles.json: default role definitions and their permission sets
- actions.json: list of canonical actions with metadata (service, sensitivity, description) — optional, but helpful for debugging and tooling
- policies/*.json: actual allow rules (resource/action/scope)
- reason_codes.json: stable reason codes for deny responses (so UI can show “why”)
- CHANGELOG.md: human-readable notes for support + customer admins

Open question: do we include “action metadata” in the shipped bundle for Private? Pros: better local debugging and “permission denied” UX. Cons: risk of drift vs code annotations.


Distribution options
Option A — Bundle embedded in images (per-service)
- Mechanism: ship bundle as a file baked into container images (or helm chart configmap) for the control plane service.
- Update: bundle changes only when upgrading images.
Pros:
- simplest operationally: upgrade = new images = new bundle
- guaranteed compatibility (in theory) because built together
Cons:
- slower to patch policy-only changes
- console/control plane might not share exact same bundle if images differ
- harder to support “bundle patch” without full upgrade (air-gapped customers often want minimal deltas)
Notes:
- We can still have “bundle is a standalone artifact” even if it’s embedded. But embedding makes provenance harder to explain.

Option B — Standalone signed artifact shipped with installer (recommended direction)
- Mechanism: bundle shipped as separate artifact alongside helm charts/images; installer places it in a well-known location and mounts into relevant pods.
- Update: installer upgrades the bundle independently (usually coupled to product upgrade, but can be patched).
Pros:
- decouples policy updates from binary updates (while still allowing compatibility checks)
- single source of truth for all services (control plane + console backend + any admin tooling)
- clearer offline signature verification story
Cons:
- more moving parts in installer (atomic updates + rollbacks)
- need careful version skew logic and UI messaging

Option C — Pull from Redwood (online) + cache locally
- Mechanism: Private control plane periodically checks Redwood endpoint to download latest compatible bundle, verify signature, apply.
Pros:
- fastest policy update cadence for connected customers
Cons:
- does not work for air-gapped (our hardest requirement)
- introduces complexity/security concerns (outbound connectivity and update channel)
Conclusion: might be additive later for “connected private,” but must not be primary.

Current leaning: Option B (standalone signed bundle), with Option A as fallback for “bundle missing” on first boot.


Signature + integrity design (offline)
Threat model (high-level): attacker or misconfiguration swaps bundle to grant excessive permissions, or corrupt bundle causes evaluator crash or unexpected allow.

Requirements:
- verify integrity and provenance offline
- avoid “accept unsigned bundle” bypass
- allow key rotation over time (bundle signing keys will rotate)

Proposed:
- Use an offline-verifiable signature on the bundle (e.g., Sigstore-style signing but without online Rekor dependency for Private).
- Bundle contains:
  - bundle.tar.zst
  - bundle.tar.zst.sig (signature)
  - bundle.tar.zst.pem (optional certificate chain) OR we ship public key(s) with the product
- Private installer has embedded Redwood public keys (or a trust store file shipped with the installer) used to verify the signature.
- On verification failure:
  - installer refuses to apply update
  - services continue using last-known-good bundle
  - emit a local admin-visible alert/event (“RBAC policy update rejected: signature invalid”)

Open questions:
- Do we allow customers to add their own signing key to “re-sign” a bundle after internal review? (Some regulated customers prefer internal signing gates.) If yes, we need a trust chain model: Redwood signs the bundle, customer signs “approval wrapper,” evaluator trusts customer key for “approved bundle hash X.”
- Key rotation: do we ship multiple public keys in trust store with explicit validity windows? (Likely yes.)


Where does the bundle live at runtime?
Constraints:
- must be readable by evaluator with low latency
- must be consistent across replicas
- must be versioned and auditable

Proposed runtime location:
- Store current bundle in a persistent volume (PV) mounted read-only into pods needing evaluation.
- Path: /etc/redwood/authz/policy-bundle/current (symlink) -> /etc/redwood/authz/policy-bundle/releases/<bundle_version>/
- Installer stages new bundle under releases/<new_version>/, verifies signature, then atomically flips symlink (or updates a ConfigMap with a pointer + triggers rollout).

Alternative:
- Use Kubernetes ConfigMap to store bundle contents.
Concerns:
- size limits + updates not atomic across pods unless careful
- not great for large bundles and frequent updates


How do services load the bundle?
Proposed:
- Evaluator library supports:
  - file-watch with debounce (for symlink flip)
  - explicit reload endpoint (admin-only) to force reload in emergency
  - metrics: current_policy_version, last_reload_success, last_reload_time
- Startup behavior:
  - if bundle present and valid: load
  - if bundle missing: fail startup with explicit error OR load embedded fallback bundle (see “fallback”)

Fallback design:
- Embed a minimal default bundle in the service binary/image ONLY for bootstrapping.
- If no external bundle found, service can start in “bootstrap mode” with minimal safe permissions:
  - only Org Admin (or initial admin) can do setup actions
  - support impersonation disabled
  - any high-risk actions require external signed bundle
This fallback is contentious: Security may prefer fail-closed. For installer-driven systems, we can probably require bundle always provided.
Action: align with Marcus + Aisha on whether fallback is acceptable.


Installer hooks (day 0 install)
Desired flow:
1) Installer gathers artifacts (images, charts, policy bundle) from customer-provided package.
2) Installer verifies policy bundle signature using embedded trust store.
3) Installer writes bundle to PV location (or host path if not k8s; some Private installs are not pure k8s).
4) Installer deploys control plane + console backend with volume mount to bundle path.
5) Installer runs a post-install “authz self-check”:
   - call a health endpoint that returns policy_version + schema_version + evaluator latency
   - run a small permission conformance test set (smoke) to ensure key admin actions are allowed for initial admin

Upgrade hook:
- Stage new bundle next to old
- Run compatibility check (see below)
- Flip pointer atomically
- Trigger rollout or SIGHUP-like reload
- Monitor for “spike in denies” (shadow-deny style) if enabled


Version skew handling
We need explicit compatibility gates because policy schema and action taxonomy evolve.

Compatibility dimensions:
1) Policy schema version vs evaluator version
2) Action name set vs service endpoints
3) Console UI expectations (showing reason codes, permission names) vs backend

Proposed rules:
- Bundle includes policy_schema_version and a required evaluator range (min_evaluator_version).
- Evaluator refuses to load bundle with incompatible schema (logs clear error; metrics reflect failure).
- Services can operate in “unknown actions” mode:
  - If an endpoint expects a permission that isn’t in the bundle: treat as deny (safe) but produce reason code ACTION_NOT_IN_BUNDLE.
  - However, this could break upgrades if bundle lags behind code. Prefer installer ensures bundle >= code’s required_bundle_version.

Code-side requirement:
- Each service build declares REQUIRED_POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSION and REQUIRED_BUNDLE_MIN_VERSION (or required action set hash).
- On startup, service checks loaded bundle compatibility and surfaces:
  - healthz/authz returning degraded status: “bundle too old for this binary”
  - explicit admin guidance: “Upgrade policy bundle to >= X or rollback service to <= Y”

Operational guidance:
- Installer should upgrade bundle before (or in same step as) upgrading services to avoid “bundle too old” denies.

Open question:
- Do we support “bundle newer than binary” gracefully? Usually yes, if schema compatible. But if bundle references actions unknown to older binaries, that’s fine; it’s a superset.


Emergency patch path (air-gapped)
Scenario: a permission bug blocks customer admins from critical action; we want to ship a policy-only patch quickly.

Constraints:
- Customer may not want full image upgrade
- Air-gapped means patch must be deliverable as a signed file via existing customer intake process

Proposed:
- Provide “policy bundle patch releases” that are still full bundles (immutable), signed with Redwood key.
- Installer supports “bundle-only upgrade” mode:
  - verify signature
  - apply bundle
  - reload services
- Document rollback: pin previous bundle version and reload.

Risks:
- If patch requires code change too, bundle-only upgrade won’t help; must be explicit in advisories.


Auditability / evidence
What we should record:
- At runtime, audit log events include policy_version + role_ids + decision_reason (Kevin’s audit logging changes).
- Additionally, Private admin audit log should record:
  - “policy bundle updated” event with:
    - old_version -> new_version
    - who initiated update (local admin, installer automation, support)
    - verification result (signature OK)
    - artifact hash

Open question:
- Where do these “policy update events” live for Private? In our audit log pipeline (local store + export) ideally, not just installer logs.


Support workflows
- Support should not ask customers to hand-edit JSON policy files.
- If we need to diagnose denies:
  - Provide a command/tool: rbacctl explain --actor <id> --action <action> --resource <...>
  - Must work offline.
  - Should output policy_version + matched rule + why deny.

- Support impersonation in Private: still under leadership decision. If allowed, it must be time-bounded and must not depend on “support pulling latest policy over the network.” (See break-glass doc in Confluence; we need a Private mapping.)


Recommendation (tentative)
Proceed with Option B: standalone signed bundle shipped with installer and mounted into services, with atomic staging + symlink flip + reload.
- Make bundle updates part of normal upgrade flow.
- Add “bundle-only upgrade” path.
- Enforce explicit compatibility checks (installer + service startup).


Open items / TODOs
1) Align on signature format + trust store approach (Jordan + Hanae + Security). Decide whether customer re-sign is a v1 requirement.
2) Define exact compatibility metadata fields in manifest (min/max control-plane version; schema version). Tie to ADR-014.
3) Decide fail-closed vs embedded fallback bundle behavior (needs Marcus/Aisha risk call).
4) Add installer tasks:
   - verify signature
   - stage/apply/rollback
   - post-install self-check
5) Define the “policy bundle updated” audit event schema for Private and where it’s stored/exported (Kevin).
6) Write a short customer-facing appendix for Private admin guide: how to check policy version, how to update bundle, rollback steps.

Appendix: rough installer pseudo-flow (upgrade)
- Input: package contains images + charts + policy_bundle_<ver>.tar.zst + .sig
- verify(policy_bundle)
- unpack to /pv/authz/releases/<ver>/
- run validate(manifest, schema)
- run compatibility_check(bundle, target_images)
- set symlink current -> releases/<ver>
- rollout restart deployments (console-backend, control-plane-api, admin-tooling)
- wait for healthz/authz OK on all
- emit audit event “policy bundle updated”
- if health fails: rollback symlink to previous + restart

Appendix: fields we should surface in /healthz/authz
- loaded_policy_version
- loaded_policy_schema_version
- signature_verified (bool)
- last_reload_time
- last_reload_success
- evaluator_p95_latency_ms
- compatibility_status (OK | BUNDLE_TOO_OLD | BUNDLE_SCHEMA_MISMATCH | SIGNATURE_INVALID | BUNDLE_MISSING)
